🔔 Introduction: what a notification system does

Hinglish samajh: Notification system users ko chhote sandesh bhejta hai: naye product, events, offers, shipping update ya security alert. Teen channel hote hain: push notification (phone ya desktop), SMS aur email. Is chapter mein hum aisa system banate hain jo roz lakhon notifications bhej sake bina deri, bina duplicate aur bina message khoye. Pehle simple design, phir uski kamiyan, aur phir message queue, workers, templates, settings, rate limiting aur tracking jodkar sudhaar.

A notification system sends short messages to users to keep them informed: a new product, an event, a special offer, a shipping update, a security alert. Almost every modern app has one, and users quickly notice if it is late, missing or annoying.

Notifications reach users in three main ways. A push notification appears on a mobile phone or a desktop even when the app is closed. An SMS message arrives as a text. An email lands in the inbox. Each channel works differently and depends on different outside providers, but the system should treat them in one consistent way.

This chapter designs a system that can send millions of notifications every day reliably, without delays and without sending the same message twice. We will start with a simple design, find its problems, and improve it with message queues, workers and a few important extras such as templates, settings, rate limiting and tracking.

The three channels

ChannelWhere it showsTypical use
Push notificationPhone or desktop notification areaBreaking news, chat message, reminders
SMSText message appOne-time passwords, urgent alerts
EmailInboxReceipts, newsletters, long messages

✨ Features

  • Sends push, SMS and email notifications.
  • Used for product news, events, offers and alerts.
  • Must be reliable at millions of messages a day.

✅ Benefits

  • Keeps users informed and engaged.
  • One reusable system for the whole company.
  • Can be tuned per channel and per user.

⚠️ Problems

  • Too many notifications annoy users, so opt-out and limits matter.
  • Depends on third-party providers that can fail.
  • Duplicate or lost messages hurt trust.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Introduction

A notification system is essential for modern applications, providing timely updates like product notifications, events, offers, and alerts. Notifications can be sent through:

  1. Push notifications (mobile or desktop),
  2. SMS messages, and
  3. Emails.

The chapter focuses on designing a scalable system capable of sending millions of notifications daily.

Interview questions and answers

What is a notification system?
A system that sends messages such as push notifications, SMS and emails to users to inform them about events, offers and alerts.
What channels does it support?
Push notifications (iOS, Android, desktop), SMS and email.
Cross question: Why not send notifications directly from each service?
Every service would duplicate the integration with providers, the opt-out logic and the rate limits. A shared system is simpler, safer and consistent.
Cross question: What makes a notification system hard?
Scale (millions per day), reliability (no lost or duplicate messages), third-party dependencies, user preferences and low latency for urgent messages.

📝 Step 1: Requirements and scale

Hinglish samajh: Requirements: teen tarah ke notifications (push, SMS, email), soft real-time delivery, iOS, Android aur desktop, client app ya server schedule se trigger, aur user opt-out. Scale: 10 million push, 1 million SMS aur 5 million email roz, yaani lagbhag 185 notifications per second ka average (meri gananaa). Asli chunauti bursts hain, jaise ek saath bhejne wala marketing campaign, jahan message queues kaam aati hain.

We agree on the following requirements. The system supports three types of notifications: push notifications, SMS messages and emails. It is a soft real-time system: notifications should arrive as soon as possible, but a small delay is acceptable when the system is under heavy load. It supports iOS devices, Android devices and desktop. Notifications can be triggered by client applications or scheduled on the server side. And users must be able to opt out: a user who disables a type of notification must not receive it.

Scale numbers: 10 million push notifications, 1 million SMS messages and 5 million emails per day. Let us turn those into rates (my own calculation): 10 million per day is about 116 per second on average, 1 million per day is about 12 per second, and 5 million per day is about 58 per second, so about 185 notifications per second in total on average. That is a modest rate, but traffic comes in bursts (for example a marketing campaign sent to everyone at the same minute), so the system must be able to absorb peaks many times higher than the average. This is exactly where message queues help.

Requirements

✨ Features

  • Push, SMS and email on iOS, Android and desktop.
  • Soft real-time delivery.
  • Opt-out support.

✅ Benefits

  • Clear scale targets: 16 million notifications per day.
  • Opt-out protects users and the company.
  • A modest average rate means the main challenge is bursts, not constant load.

⚠️ Problems

  • Bursts can be many times larger than the average.
  • Soft real time still means users notice long delays.
  • SMS has a real cost per message.

Interview questions and answers

What are the key requirements?
Support push, SMS and email on iOS, Android and desktop; soft real-time delivery; triggers from clients or server schedules; opt-out; and about 16 million notifications per day.
What does "soft real time" mean?
Notifications should arrive as quickly as possible, but a small delay is acceptable when the system is heavily loaded.
Cross question: Estimate the average notifications per second.
About 16 million per day divided by 86,400 seconds, which is roughly 186 per second, with peaks much higher.
Cross question: Why does opt-out matter?
Users must control what they receive. Respecting it avoids annoyance, complaints and legal trouble.

📮 Step 2: Channels, providers and contact information

Hinglish samajh: Hum delivery khud nahi banate, third-party services use karte hain: iOS push ke liye APNS, Android ke liye FCM, SMS ke liye Twilio ya Nexmo, aur email ke liye SendGrid ya Mailchimp. Bhejne se pehle contact information chahiye: app install ya signup par device token, phone number aur email jama karte hain. Ek user ke kai devices ho sakte hain, isliye device table alag rakhte hain. Simple design mein trigger services, ek notification server aur third-party services hote hain.

We do not build the delivery networks ourselves. We use third-party services. For iOS push notifications the provider is the Apple Push Notification Service (APNS): we send a request containing a device token and a payload (JSON) to APNS, which delivers it to the iPhone. For Android push we use Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM). For SMS we use commercial providers such as Twilio or Nexmo. For email we can run our own mail servers, but most companies use commercial services such as SendGrid or Mailchimp, which give better delivery rates and analytics.

To send a notification we first need to know where to send it. So we collect contact information when a user installs the app or signs up. We store device tokens (for push) and phone numbers or email addresses in the database. A user can have several devices, and each device has its own token, so one user can have many tokens. A common design uses two tables: a user table (user ID, email, country code, phone number) and a device table (device ID, device token, user ID, last logged in time).

The first, simple design then has three kinds of parts. Trigger services start notifications: a billing service sending a payment reminder, a shipping service sending a delivery update, or a cron job sending a scheduled message. The notification server provides APIs to send notifications, validates basic data (is the email or phone number valid?), and fetches the data needed to build the message from the database or cache. The third-party services deliver the final message to the user.

Providers by channel

ChannelProvider (examples)

Android pushFirebase Cloud Messaging (FCM)
SMSTwilio, Nexmo
EmailSendGrid, Mailchimp

TableTypical columnsUsed for

✨ Features

  • Third-party providers do the delivery.
  • Contact info is collected at install or signup.
  • A user can have many device tokens.

✅ Benefits

  • No need to build global delivery networks.
  • Providers give analytics and good delivery rates.
  • Simple first design that is easy to explain.

⚠️ Problems

  • Depends on outside providers that can be slow or down.
  • Device tokens can become invalid and must be cleaned up.
  • Contact data is sensitive and must be protected.

Interview questions and answers

How are iOS and Android push notifications sent?
iOS through the Apple Push Notification Service (APNS) and Android through Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM). You send the device token and a payload, and the service delivers it.
Why use third-party services for SMS and email?
They already have the delivery infrastructure, good delivery rates and analytics, so you avoid building and operating it yourself.
Cross question: How do you store contact information?
A user table for email and phone, and a device table with device tokens linked to the user, because one user can have several devices.
What are trigger services?
Services, microservices or cron jobs that generate events which cause notifications to be sent, for example billing reminders or shipping updates.

🚧 Problems with the first design

Hinglish samajh: Pehle design mein teen kamiyan hain. Pehli: single point of failure, kyunki sirf ek notification server hai. Doosri: scalability, kyunki database, cache aur processing ek saath bandhe hain aur alag alag scale nahi ho sakte. Teesri: performance bottleneck, kyunki notification banana aur bhejna bhaari kaam hai aur burst mein server dheema ho jaata hai. Iska hal agle lesson mein queues aur workers ke saath hai.

The first design is easy to understand, but it has three serious weaknesses. The first is a single point of failure (SPOF): there is only one notification server. If it crashes, no notification can be sent by anyone.

The second is poor scalability. Everything lives on or around one server: the database, the cache and the processing. You cannot scale the database, the cache and the sending logic separately, so growing one part means growing everything.

The third is performance bottlenecks. Building and sending a notification (rendering the page content, calling a third-party service and waiting for a response) takes time and resources. Under heavy load, such as a campaign sent to millions of users at once, the single server becomes slow, and all the notifications queue up behind each other. We need a design where the parts are independent, can be duplicated and are protected from sudden bursts.

Weaknesses and what they cause

WeaknessCauseEffect
Single point of failureOne notification serverOne crash stops all notifications
Hard to scaleDatabase, cache and processing tied to the serverCannot grow one part alone
Performance bottleneckHeavy work done on the same server in one stepSlowdowns and long delays under load

✨ Features

  • One notification server.
  • Database and cache bound to it.
  • Heavy work done synchronously.

✅ Benefits

  • Simple to build and reason about.
  • Fine for a prototype or a small app.
  • It makes the need for the improved design clear.

⚠️ Problems

  • Single point of failure.
  • Scalability limits: hard to scale the parts separately.
  • Performance bottlenecks during bursts.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Challenges in Initial Design

  • Single Point of Failure (SPOF): One notification server can crash the entire system.
  • Scalability Issues: Hard to scale databases, caches, and processing components independently.
  • Performance Bottlenecks: High resource demands for sending notifications.

Interview questions and answers

What is wrong with a single notification server design?
It is a single point of failure, it cannot scale the database, cache and processing separately, and it becomes a bottleneck under heavy load.
How would you start to fix it?
Move the database and cache out of the server, add more notification servers behind a load balancer, and decouple the heavy work with message queues and workers.
Cross question: Why is synchronous provider calling a problem?
A slow or failing provider holds up the request and everything behind it. With queues and workers, the provider call happens in the background and failures can be retried.
Cross question: Can you tolerate a single server for a small product?
Yes, early on. You adopt the improved design when volume or reliability needs grow.

🏗️ The improved design: servers, queues and workers

Hinglish samajh: Sudhre design mein chaar badlav hain: database aur cache ko notification server se bahar nikalo; kai notification servers lagao (horizontal scaling); message queues lagao jo burst mein buffer ka kaam karti hain; aur workers lagao jo queue se events uthakar third-party services ko bhejte hain. Aam taur par har channel (iOS, Android, SMS, email) ki alag queue hoti hai, taaki ek provider ki dikkat doosre ko na roke.

The improved design fixes the three problems with four changes. First, move the database and cache out of the notification server, so they can be scaled and secured separately. Second, add more notification servers and use automatic horizontal scaling, so there is no single point of failure and capacity can grow with demand. Third, introduce message queues to decouple the parts. A message queue acts as a buffer when a huge number of notifications must be sent. Fourth, add workers: servers that pull notification events from the queues and send them to the matching third-party services.

Typically there is a separate queue for each channel: one for iOS push, one for Android push, one for SMS and one for email. This way a failure or slowdown in one provider (say the SMS provider) does not block the other channels. The notification servers only put events into the queues and respond quickly; the heavy work and the slow provider calls happen in the workers, which can be scaled by adding more of them when queues grow.

Now each part has one clear job and can be scaled on its own. A burst of notifications is absorbed by the queues instead of crashing the servers, and the workers process the events at a steady speed.

How it works, step by step

  1. A trigger service calls a notification server through the load balancer.
  2. The server validates the request and puts a notification event into the queue for that channel.
  3. Workers pull events from the queues.
  4. A worker calls the right third-party service.
  5. The provider delivers the notification to the user.

✨ Features

  • Database and cache moved out of the servers.
  • Several notification servers behind a load balancer.
  • One message queue per channel, with workers.

✅ Benefits

  • No single point of failure.
  • Each part scales independently.
  • Queues absorb bursts and isolate provider problems.

⚠️ Problems

  • More components to run and monitor.
  • Delivery is asynchronous, so there is a small delay.
  • Queues themselves must be reliable.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Improved Design

  • Move databases and caches out of the notification server.
  • Introduce horizontal scaling with multiple notification servers.
  • Use message queues to decouple system components.
    • Message queues serve as buffers when high volumes of notifications are to be sent out.
  • Add workers that pull notification events from message queues and send them to corresponding third party services.

Interview questions and answers

How do you improve the first design?
Move the cache and database out, add notification servers with horizontal scaling, add message queues to decouple, and add workers that send to providers.
Why one queue per channel?
So that a slowdown or failure in one provider does not block the others, and each channel can be scaled and monitored on its own.
Cross question: What does the queue give you under a burst?
It buffers the events, so the servers stay fast and the workers process the events at their own pace.
Cross question: How do you scale workers?
Watch the queue length. When it grows, add workers; when it shrinks, remove them.

🛡️ Reliability: no data loss and no duplicates

Hinglish samajh: Notification system mein do vaade zaroori hain: koi notification khoye nahi aur ek hi notification do baar na jaye. Data loss se bachne ke liye notification data ko database (notification log) mein save karte hain aur retry mechanism rakhte hain. Duplicate rokne ke liye event ID check karte hain: pehle dekha hua ID ho to event discard, nahi to bhejo aur ID record karo. Exactly-once delivery ki guarantee nahi di ja sakti, par duplicates bahut kam kiye ja sakte hain.

In a notification system, two promises matter most. Never lose a notification and never send the same one twice (as far as possible).

Preventing data loss. A notification may be delayed or rejected by a provider, but it should rarely be lost. To achieve this, the system persists notification data in a database (a notification log) and implements a retry mechanism. If a worker fails to send, the event stays available and is retried later. This is why a notification log database sits next to the workers.

Deduplication. With queues and retries, the same event might be delivered more than once. We cannot guarantee exactly-once delivery, but we can greatly reduce duplicates with a deduplication check by event ID. When a notification event first arrives, check whether its event ID has been seen before. If it has, discard the event. If not, send the notification and record the ID. Because it is common for the same failure to repeat, deduplication saves users from receiving the same message many times.

A worker with a dedupe check and retries (C#)

public async Task Handle(NotificationEvent ev)
{
    ␀class="nu">0␀
    if (!await dedupe.TryAddAsync(ev.Id))          ␀class="nu">1␀
        return;                                     ␀class="nu">2␀

    ␀class="nu">3␀
    await log.SaveAsync(ev, status: ␀class="nu">7␀);

    ␀class="nu">4␀
    for (int attempt = class="nu">1; attempt <= class="nu">3; attempt++)
    {
        try
        {
            await provider.SendAsync(ev);          ␀class="nu">5␀
            await log.UpdateAsync(ev.Id, ␀class="nu">8␀);
            return;
        }
        catch when (attempt < class="nu">3)
        {
            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(Math.Pow(class="nu">2, attempt)));
        }
    }
    await log.UpdateAsync(ev.Id, ␀class="nu">9␀);        ␀class="nu">6␀
}

✨ Features

  • Notification log database for persistence.
  • Retry mechanism with backoff.
  • Event ID based deduplication.

✅ Benefits

  • Notifications survive crashes and provider failures.
  • Users are not spammed with duplicates.
  • Logs support auditing and debugging.

⚠️ Problems

  • Perfect exactly-once delivery is not possible, so some duplicates can still happen.
  • The dedupe store must be fast and kept small (for example with an expiry).
  • Retries can add delay and load.

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Reliability

  1. Prevent Data Loss:
  • Persist notification data in a database and implement a retry mechanism.
  • The Notification log database is included for data persistence.

Interview questions and answers

How do you prevent notifications from being lost?
Persist notification data in a database (a notification log) and retry sending when a provider fails.
How do you avoid duplicate notifications?
Check the event ID when an event arrives. If it has been seen before, discard it; otherwise send it and record the ID.
Cross question: Can you guarantee exactly-once delivery?
No. You can greatly reduce duplicates with dedupe checks, but because of failures and retries, true exactly-once delivery cannot be guaranteed.
Cross question: How long do you keep event IDs for dedupe?
Long enough to cover the longest retry window, then expire them to save space, for example for hours or a few days.

🧰 Additional components: templates, settings, rate limiting, retry, monitoring and tracking

Hinglish samajh: Production system mein chhe extra cheezein: notification templates (ek jaisa format, jaise "Hello {name}, order {id} ship ho gaya"), notification settings (user per channel opt-in ya opt-out), rate limiting (ek user ko kitne notifications), retry mechanism (provider fail ho to dobara bhejna), queue monitoring (queue badi ho to workers badhana) aur event tracking (open rate, click rate). Settings aur rate limit queue mein daalne se pehle check hote hain.

A production system adds six more pieces. Notification templates: a large system sends many notifications, and most follow the same format. A template is a pre-built layout with parameters, such as "Dear {name}, your order {id} has shipped". Templates keep the messages consistent, reduce errors and save time.

Notification settings: users get too many notifications and easily feel annoyed, so we give them control. Each user can opt in or opt out per channel (push, SMS, email) and per type. This is stored in a notification settings table (user ID, channel, opt-in flag). Before sending anything, the system checks the user's settings.

Rate limiting: to avoid overwhelming users, we limit how many notifications a user can receive in a period (see chapter 4). Retry mechanism: when a third-party service fails to send, the notification goes back to the queue and is retried a set number of times; if it still fails, an alert is sent to developers. Monitoring queued notifications: the key metric is the number of notifications in each queue; a large number means workers are too slow and more should be added. Events tracking: metrics such as open rate, click rate and engagement are important for understanding user behavior, so analytics services track them (for example through events sent to an analytics service).

Six additional components

ComponentPurposeExample
Notification templatesConsistent, fast message creation"Hello {name}, order {id} has shipped"
Notification settingsUser opt-in or opt-out per channelEmail on, SMS off
Rate limitingLimit how many notifications a user receivesAt most 3 marketing messages per day
Retry mechanismResend when a provider failsRetry 3 times, then alert
Queue monitoringScale workers when queues growAlert if the queue is above a threshold
Event trackingMeasure open rate, click rate, engagementAnalytics events

Why use notification templates?
To keep messages consistent, reduce mistakes and save time, since most notifications share the same format with different data.
How do you let users opt out?
Keep a notification settings table with the user ID, channel and opt-in flag, and check it before sending.
Cross question: Which notifications should bypass rate limits?
Critical ones such as security alerts and one-time passwords, which must not be dropped because of marketing limits.
What should you monitor?
Queue sizes (to scale workers), failures and retry counts, delivery latency and provider errors.
Why track open rate and click rate?
They show whether notifications are useful, so you can improve content, timing and frequency.

🔐 Security and the final notification flow

Hinglish samajh: Security: notification API sabke liye khuli nahi honi chahiye; push notification APIs ko appKey aur appSecret se surakshit karte hain taaki sirf verified clients hi notification bhej saken. Poora flow: service API call karti hai, notification server validate karta hai aur cache ya database se metadata laata hai, event message queue mein jaata hai, workers use uthakar third-party service ko bhejte hain, aur provider user tak pahunchata hai.

Security. The notification API must not be open to everyone, otherwise anyone could send fake notifications in your name. For push notification apps, the notes recommend appKey and appSecret to secure the push notification APIs: only verified or authenticated clients are allowed to send notifications through our APIs. In general you also protect the contact data (tokens, phone numbers, emails) with encryption and restricted access.

Now the full flow, with all the pieces. 1. A service calls the APIs of the notification servers. 2. The notification servers fetch metadata (user info, device token, settings) from the cache or database, and perform validation and checks. 3. A notification event is sent to the message queue for each channel (iOS push, Android push, SMS, email). 4. Workers pull the events from the queues. 5. Workers send the notifications to the third-party services (and update the log). 6. The third-party services deliver the notifications to the users' devices, and tracking events record the result.

How it works, step by step

  1. A service calls the notification server API (authenticated with appKey and appSecret).
  2. The server validates the request and fetches metadata from the cache or database.
  3. The server sends notification events to the message queues.
  4. Workers pull events from the queues.
  5. Workers send notifications to the third-party services.
  6. The third-party services deliver the notifications to the users.

✨ Features

  • appKey and appSecret secure the push notification APIs.
  • Metadata comes from the cache or database.
  • Queues, workers and providers deliver the message.

✅ Benefits

  • Only authorized services can send notifications.
  • Every step is decoupled and scalable.
  • Delivery results can be tracked and audited.

⚠️ Problems

  • Secrets must be stored and rotated safely.
  • More components mean more things to secure.
  • Provider keys must never be exposed to clients.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Security + Notification Flow

  • Use AppKey and AppSecret to authenticate and secure APIs for push notifications.
  1. Trigger services call APIs to send notifications.
  2. Notification servers validate requests and fetch metadata from caches or databases.
  3. Notification events are sent to message queues.
  4. Workers process events and interact with third-party services.
  5. Third-party services deliver notifications to users.

Interview questions and answers

How do you secure the notification API?
Require authentication, for example appKey and appSecret, so only verified clients can send notifications. Also protect stored contact data.
Walk me through the final notification flow.
A service calls the notification server API; the server validates and fetches metadata; an event goes to the right queue; workers pull and send it via third-party providers; the provider delivers it to the user.
Cross question: Why not call providers directly from the notification server?
Doing it through queues and workers isolates provider failures, allows retries, and absorbs bursts.
Cross question: What if a provider is down for an hour?
Events wait in the queue and in the log, workers retry with backoff, and an alert is raised. Optionally fail over to a second provider.

🚀 Key optimizations and revision

Hinglish samajh: Aakhri optimizations: horizontal scaling (zyada notification servers), message queues (processing ko alag karna), caching (bar bar use hone wala data memory mein) aur alag alag regions mein deployment. Revision table mein poore chapter ka saar hai: channels aur providers, contact info, pehla aur sudhra hua design, reliability (log, retry, dedupe), extras (templates, settings, rate limit, tracking) aur security.

The notes finish with four optimizations. Horizontal scaling: add more notification servers to share the load. Message queues: decouple processing so high volumes can be handled and slow providers do not block anything. Caching: store frequently used data (user info, device tokens, templates, settings) in a cache to reduce latency and database load. The fourth point in the notes is about delivering messages efficiently across regions (it is worded as geographic optimization): run servers and workers in several regions so that messages are processed close to the users and the providers.

✨ Features

  • Horizontal scaling, queues, caching and regional deployment.
  • A complete, decoupled architecture.
  • Opt-out, rate limits and tracking built in.

✅ Benefits

  • Handles millions of notifications per day.
  • Reliable and observable.

⚠️ Problems

  • Operating many components needs good monitoring.
  • Provider costs can grow with volume.
  • Privacy and consent rules must be followed.

Interview questions and answers

Summarize the notification system in one minute.
Trigger services call horizontally scaled notification servers, which validate, check settings and rate limits, and put events into per-channel queues. Workers pull events, deduplicate, send them through providers like APNS, FCM, SMS and email services, retry on failure, and log results. Templates, tracking, monitoring and security complete it.
What are the key optimizations?
Horizontal scaling of servers, message queues for decoupling, caching of hot data and regional deployment.
Cross question: How would you add a new channel such as WhatsApp?
Add a new queue and a worker type for that provider. The servers and the rest of the flow stay unchanged.
Cross question: How would you handle a campaign to 10 million users at once?
Spread the sends over time or across many workers, rely on the queues to absorb the burst, respect rate limits per provider and monitor queue depth.
